441.quote_or_event: “This is the road to it: to serve the Gurus and the old (teachers), to avoid throughout foolish people, to apply oneself earnestly to study, and to ponder zealously on the meaning of the Sûtras.”
441.explanation: Mahavira's discourse on the causes of carelessness names service of the gurus and the elders as the first step on the road to liberation, paired with avoiding fools.
441.tie_back: Valluvar asks the king to weigh carefully and then win the friendship of those mature in wisdom and virtue. The Jain text likewise puts deliberate attachment to the old and learned at the head of the right path.
441.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 32.3 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
441._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on seeking out the elders and wise, though the setting is a monk's path to moksha rather than a king's search for counsellors.

442.quote_or_event: “As to one who has lost his way in the wood, others who have not, (show it, thus some) teach the path which is salutary to men. Therefore (he should think): this is for my good that those who know put me right.”
442.explanation: The Sutrakritanga compares the person who has strayed to a traveller lost in a forest, and the wise to those who know the road and lead him back to safety.
442.tie_back: The kural praises counsellors who remove troubles that have already come and guard against those still to come. The Jain image shows the knowing guide rescuing a person already lost and setting him on a road that keeps him safe from then on.
442._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. It fits the remedial half of the kural well; the preventive half (guarding against future trouble) is only implied.

443.quote_or_event: “If one can obtain the privilege of living always with men of good disposition in friendship, who constantly perform acts of virtue through a succession of births, though that succession is affliction, no one will despise it when they have considered the matter.”
443.explanation: This Tamil Jain quatrain says that the friendship of the virtuous is so precious that it would make even the round of rebirth, which Jainism counts as suffering, worth accepting.
443.tie_back: Valluvar calls honouring the great and making them one's own the rarest of rare things. The Naladiyar values that same friendship above even release from the misery of rebirth.
443.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 4 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
443._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. This is a Tamil Jain text, not canonical scripture. It matches the kural's point that such friendship is supremely precious, but it does not use the language of rarity.

444.quote_or_event: “Disobedient, rough speaking, ill-behaved pupils will exasperate even a gentle teacher; but those will soon win even a hot-tempered teacher who humour him and are polite.”
444.explanation: The Uttaradhyayana's lecture on discipline teaches that it is the junior's own conduct, humble and courteous, that wins over a superior and keeps that superior's goodwill.
444.tie_back: The kural calls it the greatest strength to conduct oneself so that those greater than oneself become one's own. The Jain verse likewise makes winning the great a matter of one's own humble conduct.
444.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.13 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
444._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Good fit on winning the great through one's own conduct, but the setting is a pupil and teacher, not a ruler, and the verse says nothing of strength.

445.quote_or_event: “So a novice who has not mastered the Law, does not know the Law, not being awakened; but afterwards he knows it well through the words of the Ginas, as with his eye (the wanderer sees the way) after sunrise.”
445.explanation: The Sutrakritanga says the untrained novice is like a guide in the dark night, and that the teaching of the Jinas becomes his eye, letting him see the road as if the sun had risen.
445.tie_back: Valluvar says a king sees through his counsellors as his eyes and so must choose them with care. The Jain text likewise treats wise instruction as the eye by which one who cannot see finds the way.
445._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com; diacritics simplified ('*G*inas' given as 'Ginas'). The eye image matches, but the 'eye' here is the Jinas' teaching, not chosen counsellors, and the stress on careful selection is missing.

446.quote_or_event: “The grass near the stump of the tree will not shake with the plough of the ploughman. Feeble though they be, the anger of enemies will not come on those who have joined the society of the good.”
446.explanation: The Naladiyar compares a person who stands among the good to grass sheltered by a tree stump, which the plough passes by without uprooting.
446.tie_back: This is almost the same thought as the kural, which says enemies can do nothing to one who lives in the fellowship of the worthy. Both promise that even a weak person is safe from enemies inside that circle.
446.source: Naladiyar, ch. 18 'Good Society', stanza 8 (English tr. in The Indian Antiquary; wisdomlib.org)
446._accuracy_note: Checked word for word on wisdomlib.org. Near one-to-one match, but from a Tamil Jain didactic text rather than canonical scripture, and very close to the Kural's own milieu.

447.quote_or_event: “Any instruction the wise ones may give me in a kind or a rough way, I shall devotedly accept, thinking that it is for my benefit.” … “Wise, fearless monks consider even a rough instruction as a benefit, but the fools hate it, though it produces patience and purity of mind.”
447.explanation: Mahavira's lecture on discipline teaches welcoming correction from the wise, even when it is harsh, because it brings patience and purity, while fools resent it.
447.tie_back: The kural asks who could ruin one who keeps companions able to rebuke him. The Jain text counts that rebuke itself as a benefit and marks the wise by their readiness to welcome it.
447.source: Uttaradhyayana Sutra 1.27, 1.29 (tr. Hermann Jacobi, SBE 45, 1895; sacred-texts.com)
447._accuracy_note: Checked word for word against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com. Strong fit on valuing those who rebuke; the Kural's political frame (a king and his advisers) becomes a pupil and teacher here.

448.quote_or_event: “If admonished by a young or an old monk, by one above him or one of equal age, he should not retort against him, being perfectly free from passion; for one who is (as it were) carried away (by the stream of the Samsâra), will not get to its opposite shore.”
448.explanation: The Sutrakritanga tells the monk to accept admonition from anyone, of any age or rank, and warns that one who rejects it is carried off by the current and never reaches the far shore.
448.tie_back: Valluvar says the king with no one to rebuke him perishes even without enemies. The Jain verse likewise shows ruin coming from within, to one who refuses correction, with no outside destroyer needed.
448._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed, diacritics simplified in 'Samsâra'). Jacobi notes that the verse's wording is obscure and that he follows the commentators. The ruin here is spiritual, not political, so the fit is partial.

449.quote_or_event: “Just as they carry off a young bird whose wings are not yet grown, so many unprincipled men will seduce a novice who has not yet mastered the Law, thinking that they can get him in their power, when they have made him leave (the Gakkha).”
449.explanation: The Sutrakritanga compares a novice who leaves the community of his teachers to a fledgling that leaves the nest too early and is snatched by birds of prey.
449.tie_back: The kural says there is no stability without the support of the worthy, just as there is no profit without capital. The Jain image of the unfledged bird shows how quickly a person without that support falls.
449._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed, 'Gak*kh*a' simplified). Strong thematic fit on support as the precondition of stability, though it uses a bird image rather than the Kural's economic analogy.

450.quote_or_event: “A good man should long to live with his teacher in order to perform his duties, knowing that he who does not live with his teacher will not put an end to his mundane existence. Making manifest the conduct of the virtuous, an intelligent (monk) should not leave the (company of his teacher).”
450.explanation: The Sutrakritanga warns that leaving the company of the virtuous teacher costs nothing less than liberation itself, so the wise do not leave it.
450.tie_back: Valluvar judges giving up the friendship of the good to be ten times worse than the enmity of many. The Jain text likewise treats leaving good company as the greatest loss, since it closes the way out of samsara.
450._accuracy_note: Checked against Jacobi on sacred-texts.com (footnote marker removed). It fits the warning against leaving good company, but it has no comparison with the enmity of many and no 'tenfold' measure.
